newsitem.title: FRANCE: France sees pollution alert but no car bans.
newsitem.headline: France sees pollution alert but no car bans.

text.p: A heat wave triggered the year's first air pollution alerts in France on Tuesday, but public health officials shied from taking the politically sensitive step of slapping restrictions on car use.
Instead, officials "invited" residents of the four affected cities -- Paris, Lyon, Lille and Strasbourg -- to voluntarily limit use of their vehicles.
They also urged the elderly, small children and people with respiratory problems to limit their physical activity.
The Paris pollution monitoring authority Airparif blamed the alarming air pollution levels in the capital on a combination of heat, sunlight, car exhausts and a lack of wind.
Parif officials added that the alerts could continue for the next few days.
Pollution in the four cities was put at "level two", the midpoint on the official scale, with "level one" deemed acceptable and "level three" requiring mandatory curbs on private cars.

Corinne Lepage, environment minister in France's previous conservative government, said in a radio interview that she hoped her leftist successor, Greens leader Dominique Voynet, would "have the political courage" to restrict cars although level three had not been reached.
But Voynet's Environment Ministry did not do so, promising instead a long-term change in French transport policy.
"The conditions are not in place for implementation of emergency plans limiting car traffic," the ministry said in a printed statement.
Health-threatening pollution has become a constant problem in France's large cities, the statement added.

"It results from policies, pursued for decades, which systematically favoured the private automobile in the city. The answer to this situation lies in a long-term approach. This is the Environment Ministry's goal," the statement said.
